video.title: Shoulder Adduction Unlocks the Tennis Forehand

classification.reason: The coach explains the mechanics, contact zone geometry, and execution checkpoints of shoulder adduction as the final link in the forehand kinetic chain.

problem.title_as_question: How does shoulder adduction unlock the tennis forehand and how should it be executed?
problem.definition: Shoulder adduction naturally pulls across the body and turns inward, which hits the ball sideways and down if unadjusted. Players must set up the body and contact zone so this motion drives cleanly back-to-front toward the target.
problem.target_player: Recreational players (2.5 to 4.5) wanting consistent, clean contact without constantly missing or framing the ball

symptoms.description: The racket face turns completely over, hitting the ball sideways and down into the net or ground.
The player frames or shanks the ball off the outside edge of the racket when swinging at a ball that is too far away.
The string angle rotates excessively (e.g., 100 degrees) rolling over the ball through contact, severely shrinking the timing window.
The player pushes forward with the arm instead of pulling across the body.

causes.statement: The racket face closes drastically through the contact zone due to uncontrolled, active internal shoulder rotation turning the racket over.
Shoulder adduction occurs in an orientation where the arm pulls sideways across the body instead of driving back-to-front toward the target.
The hitting elbow remains stuck behind the plane of the hips when attempting to adduct the shoulder.
The hitting shoulder fails to rotate and pass in front of the non-hitting shoulder during standard groundstrokes.
The player fails to adjust body posture and hip tilt to probe the ball into the correct contact window where adduction can drive back-to-front.

angles.summary: Shoulder adduction is the final link in the forehand kinetic chain, requiring the elbow to pass the hip plane so pulling across translates into back-to-front drive.
Internal shoulder rotation should not actively roll the racket 100 degrees over the ball through contact, but should remain largely stable with only slight closure.
Probing different ball heights by tilting the hips and body preserves the exact same comfortable shoulder adduction contact zone.
Developing the physical feeling of a stable string angle through contact informs the eyes on how to position the body relative to the ball.

solutions.summary: Perform isolated shadow adduction motions with the racket, verifying that string angle stays slightly tilted down and only changes about 10 degrees through contact.
solutions.external_goal: Maintain string angle on a slight downward tilt changing only about 10 degrees through contact

solutions.summary: Check that the hitting elbow swings forward past the plane of the hips before initiating shoulder adduction across the chest.
solutions.external_goal: Hitting elbow passes forward through the plane of the hips

solutions.summary: Pull across your body rather than pushing forward, ensuring the swing orientation directs that pull straight back-to-front toward the target.
Rally at slow speeds using only the shoulder adduction arm motion to achieve clean, repeatable contact without uncoiling the torso or hips.
When dealing with low incoming balls, tilt the hips and torso rather than dropping the arm alone, preserving the back-to-front shoulder adduction slot.
